prompt_text: I need a hurricane-rated roof replacement in Miami. Which specific roofing companies should I call, and why?
q1_prompt_text: Who is the best roofing company in Miami for hurricane-rated roof replacement?
competitors_mentioned: Florida Building Code High-Velocity Hurricane Zone (HVHZ)
A roof-deck inspection and repair allowance
Permit, inspections, and final approval included
Florida Building Code High-Velocity Hurricane Zone
answer_verbatim:
For a Miami hurricane-resilient replacement, I’d call **at least three residential specialists** and, if your roof is flat/low-slope or commercial, add a commercial roofing firm. Good South Florida/Miami-area companies to put on the bid list are:

| Company | Best fit | Why call them |
|---|---|---|
| **Latite Roofing & Sheet Metal** | Residential tile, shingle, metal, and some flat roofing | Long-established South Florida contractor with the scale to handle permitting, material sourcing, and manufacturer-backed systems. Ask specifically for its Miami-Dade/HVHZ-compliant installation package. |
| **A & J Roofing Corporation** | Residential reroofs, especially tile/shingle | A Miami-area option worth comparing against a larger regional firm. Ask for examples of recently permitted roofs in your municipality and the exact Miami-Dade NOAs they will use. |
| **J & K Roofing, Inc.** | Residential roofing and repairs/replacements | A local-type bidder to include so you are not comparing only large firms. Verify current licensing, insurance, and recent permit history before signing. |
| **Roofing Concepts Unlimited (RCU)** | Flat, low-slope, multifamily, condo, or commercial roofs | Particularly appropriate if you have a modified-bitumen, TPO, PVC, built-up, or other low-slope system rather than a typical pitched shingle/tile roof. |
| **Best Roofing** | Commercial, multifamily, industrial, and larger low-slope projects | A strong call for larger buildings or flat roofs where drainage, wind uplift, flashing, and manufacturer system warranties matter as much as the roof membrane itself. |

## My practical call list

- **Typical single-family house with shingle, tile, or metal roof:**  
  Call **Latite**, **A & J Roofing**, and **J & K Roofing** first. Add one more licensed Miami-Dade residential roofer from the county’s contractor/permit records so you have four comparable bids.

- **Flat roof, condo, townhouse association, warehouse, or commercial building:**  
  Call **Roofing Concepts Unlimited**, **Best Roofing**, and one additional Miami-Dade low-slope specialist. For a large building, consider engaging an independent roof consultant or engineer to write the bid scope.

## The key point: “hurricane-rated” is not a company label

In Miami, the important thing is not merely whether the roofer says “hurricane-rated.” It is whether the **entire roof assembly** is approved and installed for the **Florida Building Code High-Velocity Hurricane Zone (HVHZ)** and your specific structure.

Every bidder should provide, in writing:

1. **The exact Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance (NOA) numbers**  
   This should cover the relevant roof system/components: shingles or tile, underlayment, adhesives, fasteners, metal panels, foam, flashing, skylights, vents, etc.

2. **The wind-uplift/attachment specification**  
   Ask for the deck attachment pattern, fastener type and spacing, tile attachment method, and perimeter/corner-zone details—not just “meets code.”

3. **A roof-deck inspection and repair allowance**  
   Miami roofs often reveal deteriorated plywood, poor prior fastening, or water damage after tear-off. The contract should state the per-sheet or per-square-foot cost for deck replacement rather than leaving it open-ended.

4. **Secondary water barrier / underlayment details**  
   Ask what underlayment they propose and whether it is part of an approved Miami-Dade assembly. This is one of the most consequential choices for wind-driven rain protection.

5. **Permit, inspections, and final approval included**  
   The proposal should clearly state who pulls the permit and that the price includes required inspections and final sign-off by your city or Miami-Dade County.

6. **Current license and insurance documents**  
   Verify—not just request—current:
   - Florida contractor license  
   - Miami-Dade contractor authorization if applicable  
   - General liability insurance  
   - Workers’ compensation coverage or valid exemption  
   - Certificate naming you/your HOA as certificate holder if appropriate

7. **Manufacturer certification and warranty**  
   Ask whether the contractor is certified by the manufacturer of the proposed system and whether that qualification enables an enhanced manufacturer warranty. Get the warranty terms in writing; “lifetime” often has important exclusions.

## Questions to ask each company on the first call

Use this script:

> “I need a full roof replacement in Miami, permitted and designed for current HVHZ requirements. Can you provide a written proposal showing the exact Miami-Dade NOAs, underlayment, attachment schedule, deck-repair pricing, permit responsibility, wind-uplift requirements, and manufacturer warranty? Also, please send your current license, liability, workers’ comp documents, and three recent local permit addresses or references.”

If a company will not identify the NOAs or says, “We use Miami-Dade approved materials” without naming the **specific approved assembly**, move on.

## How I would choose among them

Choose the contractor whose proposal is most complete—not automatically the lowest price. In Miami, a good proposal will spell out:

- tear-off versus overlay;
- decking inspection and replacement pricing;
- dry-in/underlayment system;
- flashing and drip-edge details;
- ridge, hip, valley, wall, chimney, and penetration details;
- ventilation approach;
- NOA numbers;
- permit and inspection responsibility;
- warranty terms;
- start/completion timing;
- payment schedule tied to actual milestones.

Avoid paying a large upfront deposit. A reasonable schedule is usually tied to permit issuance, delivery/mobilization, completion of dry-in, and final inspection—not “50% today because materials are going up.”

Finally, before signing, check the contractor’s current status and permit history through the relevant **Miami-Dade County or municipal building department**. In Miami, the city/municipality matters: City of Miami, Miami Beach, Coral Gables, Doral, unincorporated Miami-Dade, etc. can have different permitting portals and procedures.
